job.system:
You are the AI assistant for Capitol Policy Review. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: Capitol Policy Review (CPR) is a nonpartisan, nonprofit newsroom based in Washington, DC, covering science and technology legislation in Congress. We publish explainers, vote trackers, and a weekly newsletter read by policy professionals. We do not take positions on legislation; our goal is accurate, fair, and useful coverage.

Current focus: One of our biggest stories this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup, can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
**Drafting review: S. 2817 (text as amended October 6, 2026)**

I worked from the bill text alone. I can't check the statutes it references, so items that depend on outside law are marked for verification.

1. **§2(1)(A), tonnage threshold:** The 10,000-ton limit applies "by a single vessel," so a fleet of vessels each under the limit falls outside the definition. The bill also doesn't say whether tons are measured wet or dry, as nodules with sediment or as retained minerals.

2. **§2(1)(A), depth floor:** Recovery at or above 200 meters is not covered, and the bill gives no reason for the cutoff or any alternative for shallower recovery.

3. **§2(1)(A), undefined terms:** "Recovery," "mineral resources," and "seabed" are undefined. The definition doesn't reach processing at sea or discharge of sediment and tailings, which are the main environmental impacts.

4. **§2(1)(B), "the Secretary":** No agency is named, so enforcement authority is unclear. "Secretary" could mean the Secretary of Commerce (NOAA's parent department) or the Secretary of the Interior.

5. **§2(1)(B), "comparable" standard:** The Secretary can extend the definition to activities that are "comparable" in risk, but the bill sets no standard, process, notice, or appeal. That invites both operator challenges for arbitrariness and vagueness or nondelegation claims.

6. **§2(2), "U.S. person":** The definition covers citizens and state-organized corporations only. It excludes LLCs, partnerships, trusts, and foreign-incorporated entities, and it doesn't define "State" (check whether this includes territories and D.C. under 1 U.S.C. §2).

7. **§2(3) and §4, covered vessel:** "Equipped for the recovery" is undefined. The term is used only in the registry provision, so it doesn't limit the §3 prohibition, and vessels under 5,000 gross tons fall outside the registry entirely.

8. **§3(a), "in the United States":** The bill doesn't say whether this includes the territorial sea, the Exclusive Economic Zone, or the outer continental shelf. Mining on the high seas by non-U.S. persons, or by foreign operators on U.S.-flagged vessels, may fall outside the prohibition. This is one of the largest potential gaps.

9. **§3(a), scope of "engage":** The prohibition covers only "engaging in" mining. It doesn't reach financing, contracting, equipment supply, or insurance, and it doesn't bar importing, selling, or processing minerals mined elsewhere.

10. **§3(b), "exploration license":** The term is undefined. The bill doesn't say whether it must be a U.S.-issued license, whether it can include International Seabed Authority contracts, or whether it authorizes commercial-scale recovery. Verify whether the license regime under the Deep Seabed Hard Mineral Resources Act (1980) is the intended referent.

11. **§3(b), open-ended grandfathering:** Licenses issued before enactment have no expiration, cap on activity, or limit on renewal or transfer. The phrase "mining conducted under" doesn't say whether a licensee can expand operations after enactment.

12. **§3(c), environmental assessment exemption:** The exemption has no volume cap, time limit, notice, permit, or reporting requirement, and it doesn't prohibit selling the recovered material. This is the most direct route to commercial-scale "test mining."

13. **§3 (general), relationship to existing law:** The bill doesn't say how it interacts with the Deep Seabed Hard Mineral Resources Act. It has no savings, repeal, or preemption clause. Staff should confirm the current statutory framework before the markup.

14. **§4(a), "operator":** The term is undefined. The registration provision sets no deadline and doesn't say what information registration must include.

15. **§4(b), reporting:** The bill requires reports "describing the recovery activities" without specifying quantities, locations, depths, or retained material. It sets no deadline and doesn't say whether reports are public, and unregistered operators have no reporting duty at all.

16. **§§4–5, enforcement gap:** Penalties in §5 attach only to violations of §3. Failing to register, failing to file a report, or filing a false certification carries no penalty, so the registry and reporting requirements are effectively unenforceable. Counsel should consider adding explicit penalties or a cross-reference to 18 U.S.C. §1001.

17. **§5(a) and §8, conflicting effective dates:** Section 5(a) applies penalties to violations "on or after the date of enactment," but §8 delays the whole Act, including §3, for 180 days. The bill doesn't say whether conduct during that window is penalized, which invites a notice or retroactivity challenge.

18. **§5(a), penalty mechanics:** "Each day" isn't defined, so it's unclear whether penalties run per vessel, per violation, or per ton. The bill also names no enforcing agency or procedure (administrative or civil action), sets no limitations period, and provides no injunctive relief, seizure or forfeiture of vessels or minerals, citizen suit, or whistleblower provision.

19. **§5(b), criminal penalty:** "Willfully" is undefined, and the bill includes no corporate officer liability. Criminal exposure also covers only §3 violations, not the §4 reporting duties.

20. **§6, international agreement:** "Seek to negotiate" is not a binding obligation. The bill has no reporting to Congress, no consequence if negotiations fail, and no definition of "equivalent to those in section 3." It also doesn't say what happens to the domestic prohibition if an agreement is reached.

21. **§7(a), "serious harm" and the lifting standard:** "Serious harm" is undefined, so the standard for lifting the prohibition is unclear. The National Academies report has no deadline, and the bill doesn't require Congress to act within a set time, so the prohibition could persist indefinitely or be lifted without clear process.

22. **§7(a), presidential role:** A joint resolution must be presented to the President under the Presentment Clause, so lifting the prohibition would require a signature or a two-thirds override. Confirm this is the intended mechanism.

23. **§7(a) vs. §7(b), internal conflict:** Section 7(a) keeps the prohibition in force until a joint resolution passes, while §7(b) ends the entire Act after 10 years. The bill doesn't say which controls. If §7(b) governs, the prohibition lapses without any finding, and the bill has no savings clause for penalties on violations that occur before the sunset.

24. **§8, transition gaps:** The bill doesn't specify when the §4 registry and reporting duties begin. It also doesn't prevent operators from obtaining licenses between enactment and the effective date in order to claim the §3(b) grandfather protection.

**Priorities for the markup:** Items 8 (territorial reach), 12 (§3(c) exemption), 10–11 (grandfathering), 16 (unenforceable registry), 17 (effective-date conflict), and 23 (sunset conflict) look most consequential for both loopholes and legal challenge. Items 6, 13, and the statutory references in 10 and 19 should be checked with counsel or Commerce staff before publication.
